summary: You may be earning returns on your mutual funds. Whether you are building wealth is a different question. Suranjana Borthakur of Mirae Asset works through why investors chase gold after it has already run, get restless when equity goes sideways, and abandon a perfectly good plan at the worst possible moment. She also shares a lesson from the Covid crash, when being fully invested in equity meant she could not take advantage of the fall she had been waiting for.

seo.title: Mutual Fund Returns Disappointing? Here’s How Wealth Is Really Built | Suranjana Borthakur
seo.description: Suranjana Borthakur on returns versus wealth: chasing last year's winner, rebalancing, multi-asset and lifecycle funds, and SIFs explained.

takeaways.text: Good returns and real wealth are not the same thing, and the gap between them is mostly made of interruptions.
Chasing whatever did best last year, gold included, is the rear-view mirror mistake, and it is the most common one.
Being fully invested in equity sounds like conviction until a crash arrives and you have nothing left to buy it with.
Rebalancing is the mechanism that makes you sell high and buy low without having to feel brave about it.
Your goals and your horizon decide the portfolio. Fund selection is the last decision, not the first.

fork.decision: One asset has run hard and another is flat. Follow the winner, or rebalance?

points.text: Momentum is real, and the asset that is working is working for reasons that do not vanish overnight.
Sitting in something that has gone nowhere for two years tests anybody's patience.
Selling what is working to buy what is not feels like the opposite of investing.
Buying gold after the rally is buying the news, and the return you are chasing has already happened.
A portfolio with nothing in reserve cannot act when a crash hands it an opportunity, which is the Covid lesson in the episode.
Rebalancing forces the sell-high, buy-low behaviour that almost nobody manages on instinct.

fork.pick: Rebalance, because the discipline is doing something your instincts will not. The portfolio that can take advantage of a fall is the one that was not fully committed before it.
